guides.title: Initialization, access, and property contracts
guides.summary: Read initializer and property syntax precisely, protect construction invariants, and expose only the API another module can actually use.

sections.title: A public struct needs a deliberate construction API
sections.html:
Kotlin primary constructors make a data class's construction shape visible in its declaration. Swift structs often synthesize a memberwise initializer from stored properties instead. For struct Position { var x: Int; var y: Int }, Swift supplies Position(x: 2, y: 3) when no custom initializer in the primary declaration suppresses synthesis. This is a value-construction convenience, not Kotlin data-class generation: it does not automatically add every equality or copying behavior.

Access is a common surprise. Even a public struct with public stored properties does not receive a public synthesized memberwise initializer. The synthesized initializer is normally internal, with private/fileprivate stored-property details capable of restricting it further. Write an explicit public initializer for clients in another module. Defining a custom initializer in an extension can preserve synthesized initializers that defining it in the primary struct body would suppress; use that distinction deliberately.

public struct Badge {
    public let title: String
    private let normalizedKey: String

    public init(title: String) {
        self.title = title
        self.normalizedKey = title.lowercased()
    }
}

public init makes construction callable across modules. title: is the caller's label; self.title distinguishes the property from the parameter. Every stored property receives a value. The private key is an implementation detail, not another public argument. Lowercasing here is synthetic storage behavior, not a universal locale-aware identity policy.

sections.title: Visibility is separate from mutability and isolation
sections.html:
The default access level is internal: other files in the same module can use the declaration. A SwiftPM package can contain multiple modules, so internal does not mean every target in the package. public exposes an API to importing modules. open adds permission to subclass an exposed class or override an exposed overridable member outside its defining module. Public classes remain usable externally without granting that external subclassing permission.

fileprivate restricts access to the source file. private restricts it to the enclosing declaration and eligible extensions of that declaration in the same file; it is not simply a synonym for file scope. Modern Swift also has package access for a package boundary, but that does not replace the internal/public distinction. Public signatures cannot expose types that are less accessible than the API requires.

public private(set) var count permits a public read while limiting assignment through the setter. A let class reference cannot be reassigned, but its object may still mutate. None of these access keywords creates a lock or an actor boundary. Kotlin's internal uses Kotlin module/build conventions, and Java package access is not Swift file access. Read the actual Swift target boundary before porting an assumption about who can construct, mutate, subclass, or call an object.

sections.title: Designated initializers go up; convenience initializers go across
sections.html:
Classes support designated and convenience initializers. A designated initializer establishes that class's stored state and delegates to a designated initializer of its immediate superclass when one exists. A convenience initializer delegates to another initializer on the same class with self.init, eventually reaching a designated path. Structs can also delegate with self.init, but they have no superclass or convenience/designated hierarchy.

class NamedRecord {
    let name: String
    required init(name: String) { self.name = name }
    convenience init() { self.init(name: "Synthetic") }
}
final class TaggedRecord: NamedRecord {
    let tag: Int
    init(name: String, tag: Int) {
        self.tag = tag
        super.init(name: name)
    }
    required convenience init(name: String) {
        self.init(name: name, tag: 0)
    }
}

TaggedRecord assigns its own tag before calling super. The required convenience initializer routes the superclass-required construction shape to that full path. required obliges subclasses to provide the initializer, either by permitted inheritance or implementation; it does not mean the caller must invoke it. You do not add override when implementing an initializer already marked required. In contrast, overriding a nonrequired superclass designated initializer uses override init.

Initializers have special inheritance rules; they are not inherited exactly like ordinary methods. Read the complete initializer set before assuming a convenience overload exists on a subclass. The active hosting-controller wrapper explicitly delegates its convenience builder initializer to its public root-view initializer, illustrating this distinction without establishing every caller's lifecycle.

sections.title: Establish storage before exposing a usable object
sections.html:
Class initialization has two phases: stored properties throughout the hierarchy are established, then customization can use the initialized instance. A subclass must initialize its own introduced storage before delegating upward, and must not overwrite inherited storage before the superclass initializes it. A convenience initializer delegates before assigning properties. Using instance methods, reading unfinished instance state, or allowing self to escape prematurely breaks the safety model. Kotlin superclass/constructor ordering is a helpful comparison, but Swift checks its own delegation and definite-initialization rules.

A failable initializer, spelled init?, returns an optional constructed value. Returning nil signals failure; no half-built value is returned. A throwing initializer reports a typed error through throws and the caller uses try. Choose absence when the caller only needs “not constructible”; choose an error when the reason matters. A failable UIKit coder initializer that traps because archival construction is unsupported expresses a programmer restriction, not ordinary validation failure.

struct PositiveCount {
    let value: Int
    init?(_ value: Int) {
        guard value > 0 else { return nil }
        self.value = value
    }
}
enum LabelError: Error { case empty }
struct NonEmptyLabel {
    let value: String
    init(validating value: String) throws {
        guard !value.isEmpty else { throw LabelError.empty }
        self.value = value
    }
}

The underscore removes PositiveCount's external label. validating: remains NonEmptyLabel's external label. Guard exits early so the remaining path has the required invariant. try? converts an error to absence and discards its reason; use that only when intentional.

sections.title: Stored, computed, lazy, and observed properties do different work
sections.html:
A stored property owns a value in the instance. A computed property runs a getter and optionally a setter; it does not supply storage merely because it has property syntax. A read-only computed property can omit get. In a setter, newValue names the proposed value unless you choose another name. Accessing a computed property repeatedly can repeat expensive work.

lazy var defers its stored value's creation until first access. It must be var, and reading a lazy property of a struct can require mutation, making that access unsuitable through an immutable struct binding. Initialization is not a general concurrent once-only guarantee; choose synchronization/isolation separately. A lazy closure can also capture its owner and create an ownership issue.

struct QuantityDraft {
    var quantity = 0 {
        willSet { print("next: \(newValue)") }
        didSet { print("previous: \(oldValue)") }
    }
    var doubled: Int { quantity * 2 }
    lazy var initialCaption: String = "First read: \(quantity)"
}

WillSet runs before assignment and didSet afterward; observers can run even for a same-value assignment. Ordinary direct assignments establishing a type's own stored properties during initialization do not fire its observers, while inherited/delegated setter paths need careful interpretation. Observers are not constructors or transactional validation. Here the lazy caption captures the first accessed quantity, then remains stored while doubled reflects each current quantity. Keep such snapshot semantics explicit rather than accidentally displaying stale derived state.

exercise.brief: Construct synthetic values and subclass instances, then predict each optional, error, access boundary, and property update before checking it in a scratch Swift target.
steps: Add the declarations to a scratch target; construct Badge and TaggedRecord through their declared APIs.
Compare PositiveCount(0) and PositiveCount(3), then catch the empty-label error explicitly.
Read a QuantityDraft's lazy caption at quantity two, change quantity to four, and compare caption with doubled.
Explain how a separate importing module would differ from a second file in the same module.
acceptance: TaggedRecord(name: "A") produces tag zero, while the full initializer preserves its explicit tag.
Invalid count is nil; invalid label throws LabelError.empty without being silently mapped to success.
The lazy caption remains the first-read snapshot while doubled reflects current quantity.
The explanation identifies the explicit public initializer and distinguishes internal, public, open, and restricted setters.
exercise.solution:
The declarations above are standalone Swift. Keep a mutable draft binding because accessing its lazy property mutates its storage. This worked check records value semantics, not a production feature.

let badge = Badge(title: "Demo")
assert(badge.title == "Demo")
let record = TaggedRecord(name: "A")
assert(record.name == "A" && record.tag == 0)
assert(TaggedRecord(name: "B", tag: 7).tag == 7)
assert(PositiveCount(0) == nil)
assert(PositiveCount(3)?.value == 3)
do {
    _ = try NonEmptyLabel(validating: "")
    assertionFailure("Expected validation error")
} catch LabelError.empty {
    // The expected reason remains observable.
} catch {
    assertionFailure("Unexpected error")
}
var draft = QuantityDraft()
draft.quantity = 2
let caption = draft.initialCaption
draft.quantity = 4
assert(draft.doubled == 8)
assert(draft.initialCaption == caption)
assert(caption == "First read: 2")

For an access audit, explain that another file in the same target still sees internal declarations, whereas an importing target needs the public API. Badge's private normalizedKey is unavailable to either ordinary outside caller. A public class would be usable across that boundary; an open class/member additionally permits external inheritance/overriding. These statements are language contracts, not a claim that a separate module experiment or a client build ran. Add that scratch-module experiment when studying packaging in sessions 043–044.

guides.title: Generics, associated types, opaque results, and protocol dispatch
guides.summary: Preserve the type relationships a caller needs, understand what any and some hide, and distinguish protocol requirements from extension-only helpers.

sections.title: A generic parameter is a relationship, not an Any box
sections.html:
Your Kotlin experience with fun <T> is a useful start: Swift func identity<T>(_ value: T) -> T ties input and output to the same chosen type. The caller can receive an Int when it passes an Int without recovering it by a cast. T is a local type parameter, not a globally defined class and not a promise about every operation a value supports.

A constraint such as T: Equatable authorizes equality through that protocol. where expresses additional relationships, including same-type requirements such as A.Element == B.Element. A colon names a conformance/subtype constraint; the double equals in a where clause requires matching types, rather than comparing runtime values. Write only constraints that the implementation actually needs.

func same<T: Equatable>(_ left: T, _ right: T) -> Bool {
    left == right
}

The two T parameters must fit the same chosen type, and the return is Bool. Calling same(2, 2) works; mixing an Int variable and a String variable does not satisfy that signature. Swift generics can specialize, but do not transplant JVM type-erasure or reified-parameter assumptions. Constraints do not automatically make mutable objects thread-safe or Sendable. The active sequence helpers use constraints to authorize sorting and hashing while keeping output element types intact.

sections.title: An associated type belongs to a conformance
sections.html:
A protocol's associatedtype names a type supplied by each conforming implementation. The source's element relationship is part of the contract, not an arbitrary runtime payload label. Modern Swift permits a primary associated type list, used below to make Element convenient to constrain. The angle brackets on the protocol declaration identify associated types; they do not turn protocol conformance into ordinary generic-class instantiation.

protocol ItemSource<Element> {
    associatedtype Element
    var items: [Element] { get }
}
struct ArraySource<Value>: ItemSource {
    let items: [Value]
}
func first<S: ItemSource>(_ source: S) -> S.Element? {
    source.items.first
}
func firstMatches<L: ItemSource, R: ItemSource>(
    _ left: L, _ right: R
) -> Bool where L.Element == R.Element, L.Element: Equatable {
    guard let l = left.items.first, let r = right.items.first else {
        return false
    }
    return l == r
}

ArraySource's property lets the compiler infer its Element as Value. S.Element refers to the concrete source conformance's associated type. The question mark permits an empty source. FirstMatches allows different source implementations while requiring their element types to match and support equality. Guard unwraps both optional first values; this contract returns false if either is absent. No Any cast is needed. Primary associated types and constrained existential syntax require a sufficiently modern compiler, including Swift 5.7 onward; that is a language-tooling requirement, not a new runtime resource in an array.

sections.title: Any stores a protocol-conforming value behind a boundary
sections.html:
any ItemSource is an existential type: a value can hold some conforming implementation while exposing the protocol boundary. A collection of these values can hold sources with different concrete types and different element types. That flexibility can be useful for a heterogeneous registry, but it loses relationships the caller did not constrain. It is not the same thing as Swift's unrestricted Any.

let heterogeneous: [any ItemSource] = [
    ArraySource(items: [1, 2]),
    ArraySource(items: ["a", "b"])
]
let knownIntegers: any ItemSource<Int> = ArraySource(items: [3, 4])
let integer: Int? = knownIntegers.items.first

The first array deliberately erases a common element relationship. The constrained existential keeps Element equal to Int while hiding the concrete source implementation. Therefore any does not universally erase every useful type fact. Some protocol operations involving Self or associated types remain restricted when the relationship is unknown. Modern Swift can implicitly open some existentials when passing them into generic functions; do not assume either that every operation is forbidden or that every generic relationship can be reconstructed.

Use an existential when storing interchangeable implementations behind a real API boundary. Use a generic when callers need preserved type relationships. Boxing and dispatch costs depend on representation and optimization; choose from behavior first, then measure a relevant hot path. The Kotlin interface analogy helps with abstraction, but Swift's existential opening and associated-type rules need their own reasoning.

sections.title: Some hides an implementation while preserving its identity
sections.html:
In a return position, some describes an opaque result: the function chooses a concrete implementation, and callers use its declared capabilities without naming that implementation. All return paths must satisfy the same underlying type for the relevant generic substitution. Returning an integer source on one branch and a string source on another is not made valid by spelling some. An existential can accommodate changing implementations under its boundary; an opaque result keeps a stronger identity relationship.

func integers() -> some ItemSource<Int> {
    ArraySource(items: [2, 4, 6])
}
func itemCount(_ source: some ItemSource) -> Int {
    source.items.count
}
protocol ReplacingTitle {
    func replacingTitle(_ title: String) -> Self
}
struct Note: ReplacingTitle {
    let title: String
    func replacingTitle(_ title: String) -> Self {
        Self(title: title)
    }
}

Parameter-position some is shorthand for a generic parameter under a constraint. Two separate some parameters do not automatically mean the same type; name a shared T when you need that relationship. Self refers to the conforming/current type, whereas lowercase self is the current instance. Note's method constructs a Note through Self and retains that return relationship. This does not promise deep copying or make all class factories trivial; subclassing and construction requirements add constraints.

sections.title: Only declared requirements participate in the protocol contract
sections.html:
A protocol extension can provide a default implementation of a declared requirement, or add a helper absent from the protocol declaration. Those have different dispatch behavior. For a requirement, a conformance supplies a witness that protocol/generic calls use. An extension-only helper is selected from the static protocol constraint, not automatically replaced by a concrete type's same-named method.

protocol Greeting { func message() -> String }
extension Greeting {
    func message() -> String { "default" }
    func decoration() -> String { "extension helper" }
}
struct CustomGreeting: Greeting {
    func message() -> String { "custom requirement" }
    func decoration() -> String { "concrete helper" }
}
func throughGeneric<G: Greeting>(_ value: G) -> [String] {
    [value.message(), value.decoration()]
}

A direct CustomGreeting call selects its concrete decoration. Through the generic Greeting constraint, message uses the custom requirement implementation while decoration selects the extension helper. Calling through any Greeting has the same distinction here. Kotlin extension functions provide a useful static-dispatch analogy, but Swift additionally has default requirement witnesses. With class hierarchies, an inherited conformance that already selected an extension default does not necessarily acquire a new witness because a subclass adds a same-named method. Put customization in a real requirement and design any superclass override path explicitly. Test calls through the actual boundary, not just concrete instances.

exercise.brief: Use the synthetic sources and greetings to predict which type relationships and implementations remain visible through concrete, generic, existential, and opaque boundaries.
steps: Call first and firstMatches with two Int sources, then verify the empty-source policy.
Use integers() as an opaque source and knownIntegers as a constrained existential without downcasts.
Compare direct, generic, and existential message/decoration calls.
Explain which change would make decoration customizable through the protocol contract.
acceptance: Generic first returns the associated element type as an optional, and mismatched element types cannot satisfy firstMatches.
Opaque and constrained existential examples retain Int as their element contract.
Generic/existential decoration returns the extension helper; message returns the declared requirement's custom implementation.
The answer distinguishes Self from self and proposes a protocol requirement when polymorphic customization is intended.
exercise.solution:
These checks are standalone Swift when combined with the guide's declarations. They verify behavior at the boundary rather than mirroring compiler machinery.

let source = ArraySource(items: [2, 4])
let typedFirst: Int? = first(source)
assert(typedFirst == 2)
assert(firstMatches(source, ArraySource(items: [2, 8])))
assert(!firstMatches(source, ArraySource(items: [Int]())))
let opaque = integers()
assert(first(opaque) == 2)
assert(itemCount(knownIntegers) == 2)
let greeting = CustomGreeting()
assert(greeting.decoration() == "concrete helper")
assert(throughGeneric(greeting) == ["custom requirement", "extension helper"])
let erased: any Greeting = greeting
assert(erased.message() == "custom requirement")
assert(erased.decoration() == "extension helper")
let changed: Note = Note(title: "Before").replacingTitle("After")
assert(changed.title == "After")

To make decoration part of polymorphic customization, add func decoration() -> String to Greeting itself. The extension may still provide its default, but CustomGreeting's implementation now fulfills a declared requirement. Recheck the generic/existential results after that deliberate API change. Avoid changing the original example while predicting it, because the comparison depends on decoration being extension-only.

A separate explanatory answer should state that an existential hides the implementation under a protocol boundary, an opaque result hides a chosen concrete result while retaining its identity, and a generic names relationships among its inputs/outputs. The example uses modern language syntax without asserting every checkout target uses the same Swift mode. It does not demonstrate all associated-type, variance, inheritance, or ABI cases; those are further study once the small contract is clear.

guides.title: Callback ownership, notifications, queues, and actor boundaries
guides.summary: Give delegates, observation tokens, actions, and asynchronous work explicit owners; separate registration, execution context, cancellation, and stale-result protection.

sections.title: A delegate is a capability with a separate owner
sections.html:
An Android listener connects an event producer to a receiver; a Swift delegate often expresses that capability as a protocol. The delegate property does not decide how long the receiver should live. Many UIKit-style delegates are weak to avoid a cycle, so another owner must retain the receiver. Assigning a newly constructed temporary receiver to a weak property can make the callback disappear immediately. A protocol alone does not imply weak retention or a particular callback thread.

@MainActor
protocol DraftDelegate: AnyObject {
    func didChange(id: String)
}
@MainActor
final class DraftSource {
    weak var delegate: (any DraftDelegate)?
    func publish(_ id: String) { delegate?.didChange(id: id) }
}

AnyObject restricts conformers to reference types, enabling weak storage. The parentheses group the existential before the optional question mark. Optional chaining makes a missing delegate a no-op. id: remains the method's external argument label; publish's underscore removes its label. Both producer and protocol are MainActor-isolated, so this synthetic contract deliberately requires UI-domain calls. A legacy delegate lacking actor annotations needs a separate adaptation decision.

Kotlin listeners and callbackFlow can serve similar product roles, but a Flow bridge needs registration in its producer and cleanup in its termination path. A weak delegate is neither a flow nor cancellation: it can stop delivery while the producer continues expensive work. Name registration and producer stopping separately.

sections.title: Block notification observers need the returned token
sections.html:
NotificationCenter's block registration returns an opaque observer token. The center retains its registration and copied block until removal. Dropping your token variable does not reliably remove that registration; keep the token or a wrapper that removes it. Removing the receiver object instead of the returned token does not remove the corresponding block registration. A block capturing its token-owning screen strongly can keep that screen alive, preventing deinit cleanup from solving the cycle.

import Foundation

extension Notification.Name {
    static let syntheticCount = Notification.Name("example.course.count")
}
final class BlockObservation {
    private let center: NotificationCenter
    private let token: any NSObjectProtocol

    init(center: NotificationCenter, receive: @escaping @Sendable (Int) -> Void) {
        self.center = center
        self.token = center.addObserver(
            forName: .syntheticCount, object: nil, queue: nil
        ) { note in
            let value = note.userInfo?["count"] as? Int ?? 0
            receive(value)
        }
    }
    func stop() { center.removeObserver(token) }
    deinit { center.removeObserver(token) }
}

This Foundation example requires no UI framework. @escaping permits retaining receive; @Sendable constrains captures used across delivery contexts. The cast and nil-coalescing expression extracts a synthetic Int, with a deliberately declared zero fallback. Real payloads need an explicit validation contract. The wrapper owns cleanup and is not declared Sendable; keep its lifecycle under an appropriate owner. Explicit stop ends the intended subscription sooner than object destruction, while deinit is a fallback. The active notification utility also wraps token removal in deinit; that source pattern does not supply UI isolation.

sections.title: Selector observation and target-action have different registrations
sections.html:
The selector overload registers an observer object and an Objective-C-compatible method instead of returning a block token. Its syntax includes #selector(Adapter.receive(_:)), and the method normally uses @objc on an NSObject-backed adapter. The underscore/colon represents the method's argument shape, not a String naming an arbitrary Swift closure. Remove this registration with the observer object, optionally narrowing by name and sender. Keep block-token removal and selector-object removal distinct.

On iOS 9/macOS 10.11 and later, selector-based observers have automatic cleanup when the observer deallocates under the documented API behavior. That is not the block API's lifetime rule and does not express a shorter feature subscription. Explicitly remove registration when the intended observation ends. Selector delivery also does not prove UI-thread execution; an adapter still needs a safe UI-domain hop.

UIKit target-action connects controls to event-specific actions. For example, button.addTarget(handler, action: #selector(Handler.tap(_:)), for: .touchUpInside) requires a compatible method and a retained handler owner; UIControl does not retain the target for you. A nil target uses responder-chain routing rather than a missing weak delegate. Remove obsolete targets/actions when their intended connection ends. Closure-based UIAction has different closure-retention concerns, so do not assume every action API shares selector target ownership. These UIKit expressions are syntax references; the complete runnable examples here use synthetic Foundation and delegate types.

sections.title: Posting context is not an actor-isolation guarantee
sections.html:
With a nil operation queue, a block notification observer runs synchronously on the posting thread. Another configured queue changes delivery context, and notifications can arrive from background work. Even choosing the main operation queue should not be confused with a compiler-declared MainActor contract. Extract a small Sendable payload while in the callback, then marshal deliberately to the owner. Passing an arbitrary Notification/userInfo graph into a task can carry unsafe references across the boundary.

@MainActor
final class CounterScreen {
    private(set) var count = 0
    var onReceive: (@MainActor (Int) -> Void)?
    private var observation: BlockObservation?
    private var generation = 0

    func start(center: NotificationCenter) {
        stop()
        let expected = generation
        observation = BlockObservation(center: center) { [weak self] value in
            Task { @MainActor [weak self] in
                guard let self, self.generation == expected else { return }
                self.count = value
                self.onReceive?(value)
            }
        }
    }
    func stop() {
        generation += 1
        observation?.stop()
        observation = nil
    }
}

The explicit actor hop updates state under MainActor. Weak captures avoid the center/block/screen retention cycle. Stop advances a generation before removal: a callback already scheduled for the UI cannot commit under an obsolete generation, including after restart. The onReceive hook supports a completion-gated synthetic check. This short Task is unstructured; the guard protects publication but does not cancel arbitrary long-running work. For that work, define retained handles or a structured scope and cooperative cancellation.

sections.title: GCD schedules closures; groups count completion
sections.html:
A DispatchQueue is a scheduling/ordering boundary, not necessarily a dedicated thread. Main-queue work executes on the main thread; a serial background queue runs submitted work one at a time. QoS describes scheduling intent rather than a completion deadline. Async submission returns before work finishes; sync submission waits and can execute work as permitted by the queue. A callback does not acquire MainActor isolation just because it is named “completion.”

import Dispatch

func legacyBatch(completion: @escaping @Sendable () -> Void) {
    let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "example.course.batch", qos: .utility)
    let group = DispatchGroup()
    for index in 0..<2 {
        group.enter()
        queue.async {
            defer { group.leave() }
            print("Synthetic job \(index)")
        }
    }
    group.notify(queue: .main, execute: completion)
}

Enter increments outstanding work, leave balances it, and notify schedules completion after the outstanding count reaches zero. Defer covers synchronous exits. For an API starting a later callback, leaving when request creation returns would count only scheduling; leave at the actual callback outcome. Exactly-once balance matters on failures and cancellation too.

A group does not collect typed results, propagate errors, cancel children, or synchronize concurrent writes to a results array. A structured task group provides a scoped lifetime and child results under its own cancellation rules. Dispatching a callback and launching Task from it does not automatically turn the entire legacy operation into structured concurrency.

sections.title: Waiting can prevent the very completion you need
sections.html:
A DispatchSemaphore wait decrements an available permit or blocks the calling thread until a signal/timeout permits progress. DispatchGroup.wait also blocks. Neither is Swift await. Blocking a cooperative executor while waiting for another task can prevent necessary work from making progress; avoid using semaphore wrappers to turn async APIs into synchronous calls. A continuation bridge suspends instead, but still requires exactly-once resumption and a designed cancellation/completion race.

Calling DispatchQueue.main.sync while already executing on the main queue deadlocks. A background queue synchronously waiting for main can also deadlock when main is waiting for that background work. Do not “fix” the cycle by guessing thread availability or adding another queue. Remove the blocking dependency and represent completion asynchronously. MainActor.run is for an awaited synchronous actor-isolated state update, not a blocking substitute for an asynchronous workflow.

Teardown has several parts: unregister delivery, stop owned producer work, invalidate stale commits, and release retained receivers/resources. Removing an observer does not cancel a callback or Task already in flight. A weak delegate does not stop its producer. Canceling a task requests cooperation rather than killing a thread. The runnable examples demonstrate registration and publication rules; they do not implement every callback cancellation adapter. Test route exit, repeated start/stop, and background posting with controlled completion signals, not sleeps that merely hope work has finished.

exercise.brief: Verify synthetic delegate delivery, block-observer cleanup, and completion-gated actor marshaling; explain why a blocking group/semaphore wait would change the design.
steps: Combine the declarations in a scratch Apple-platform Swift target, retaining the delegate receiver explicitly.
Post a synthetic count notification and await a completion signal from the MainActor receiver.
Stop observation, post again, and confirm no new delivery; reason through a pre-stop queued callback and restart generation.
Await legacyBatch through a checked continuation without blocking main or a cooperative task thread.
acceptance: A retained delegate receives an ID; clearing the delegate stops delivery without claiming producer cancellation.
The notification payload crosses as Int and visible state changes only under MainActor.
Stop removes the block token and advances a generation before any stale publication can commit.
The group check completes through notify and no semaphore/group wait or main.sync is introduced.
The explanation distinguishes selector cleanup, block-token removal, target ownership, and in-flight work.
exercise.solution:
This Foundation/Dispatch check uses explicit completion gates. Run the async function from an async scratch entry point with await checkCallbacks(); do not block a main thread to wait for it.

@MainActor
final class Recorder: DraftDelegate {
    var ids: [String] = []
    func didChange(id: String) { ids.append(id) }
}

@MainActor
func checkCallbacks() async {
    let source = DraftSource()
    let receiver = Recorder()
    source.delegate = receiver
    source.publish("synthetic-a")
    assert(receiver.ids == ["synthetic-a"])
    source.delegate = nil
    source.publish("synthetic-b")
    assert(receiver.ids == ["synthetic-a"])

    let center = NotificationCenter()
    let screen = CounterScreen()
    screen.start(center: center)
    await withCheckedContinuation { (done: CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>) in
        screen.onReceive = { value in
            guard value == 7 else { return }
            screen.onReceive = nil
            done.resume()
        }
        center.post(name: .syntheticCount, object: nil, userInfo: ["count": 7])
    }
    assert(screen.count == 7)
    screen.stop()
    center.post(name: .syntheticCount, object: nil, userInfo: ["count": 99])
    assert(screen.count == 7)

    await withCheckedContinuation { (done: CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>) in
        legacyBatch { done.resume() }
    }
}

The receiver binding keeps the weak delegate alive. Notification posting executes the nil-queue callback synchronously, but the UI Task finishes later; the continuation waits for actual receipt. Clearing onReceive before resumption prevents that test callback from resuming twice. After stop, another post has no registered block to schedule. An already queued callback instead checks its captured generation, so removal and stale-publication protection remain distinct mechanisms.

The legacy group path leaves each entered operation and uses notify to resume once. It does not propagate arbitrary errors or cancellation; a production adapter needs those additional contracts. For background posting, move only the synthetic post into a controlled worker and retain the same receiver completion gate. For selector/target-action practice, use the documented registration shape in a suitable NSObject/UIKit target and verify its owner/lifetime separately.
